flawed_step: Step 3: The equality P(A×B)=μ(A)ν(B) is asserted without independence and is not implied by the marginals.
counterexample: Let B be a fair Bernoulli random variable. The pairs (B,B) and (B,1−B) both have fair Bernoulli marginals, but their joint distributions differ: P((B,B)=(0,0))=1/2, whereas P((B,1−B)=(0,0))=0.
assessment_summary:
1. Suppose two joint distributions P and Q have the same one-dimensional marginals μ and ν. — Justified: this is the standard setup for attempting to prove uniqueness.
2. For every measurable A and B, P(A×R)=Q(A×R)=μ(A) and P(R×B)=Q(R×B)=ν(B). — Justified: these equalities are precisely what equality of the marginals means.
3. Assert that P(A×B)=μ(A)ν(B)=Q(A×B) for all measurable A,B. — Not justified: this product formula requires independence of the two coordinates, which is not assumed or implied by knowledge of the marginals.
4. If P and Q agreed on all measurable rectangles, then they would agree on the generated product σ-algebra. — Justified as a measure-uniqueness principle, but it cannot be applied here because Step 3 did not establish agreement on rectangles.
5. Conclude that P=Q and hence that the marginals uniquely determine the joint distribution. — Not justified: the needed rectangle equality is unavailable due to the failure of Step 3.
6. To test the claim, let B be a fair Bernoulli variable and define U=(B,B) and V=(B,1−B). — Justified: both are well-defined random pairs.
7. Both coordinates of U and both coordinates of V have the fair Bernoulli distribution. — Justified: B and 1−B each take 0 and 1 with probability 1/2.
8. The joint laws differ because P(U=(0,0))=1/2 while P(V=(0,0))=0. — Justified by direct evaluation of the two definitions.
9. Therefore two identical one-dimensional marginals can correspond to different joint distributions, so the statement is false. — Justified by Steps 6–8.
